text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests that measure the amount of glucose (sugar) in your blood.
snippet_highlighted_words: using specific blood tests that measure the amount of glucose (sugar) in your blood

text_blocks.snippet: Doctors use several official blood tests, as outlined by the American Diabetes Association:

list.snippet: A1C Test: Measures your average blood sugar level over the past two to three months. A result of 6.5% or higher on two separate tests means you have diabetes. No fasting is required for this test.

Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: Measures your blood sugar after you do not eat or drink anything except water for at least eight hours. A level of 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher indicates diabetes.

Random Plasma Glucose Test: Checks your blood sugar at any time of day. A level of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher combined with classic symptoms (like extreme thirst, frequent urination, or unexplained weight loss) suggests diabetes.
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): Measures your blood sugar two hours after you drink a special sugary liquid. A level of 200 mg/dL or higher confirms diabetes.

text_blocks.snippet: Except for clear cases with severe symptoms, doctors usually repeat an abnormal test on a different day to confirm a diagnosis. You can learn more about official evaluation guidelines from the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.
